title: My PC restarts by itself
summary: Distinguishes blue screen crashes, overheating, power supply faults and Windows Update restarts, which all look the same from a distance.

what_sees.question: What do you see when the restart happens?
what_sees.help: The first thing to check is whether Windows logged a crash. Open Reliability Monitor to see.

options.label: A blue screen with a stop code appears first
No blue screen, it just restarts
It restarts during games or heavy work
It restarts and everything smells hot

stop_code_present.question: Do you know which stop code it shows?
stop_code_present.help: We have full repair guides for over 90 stop codes, including the ones you are seeing on laptops with new hardware.

options.label: Yes, I have the code or name
No, I cannot read it in time

update_restart.question: Does the restart happen at a similar time each day, or right after Windows tells you it finished updating?
update_restart.help: Scheduled restarts after updates happen at a set time. Crashes are random and usually follow a pattern of activity instead.

options.label: It happens after an update message, at a set time

reliability_history.question: What does Reliability Monitor show for the times it restarted?
reliability_history.help: Press Win plus R, type perfmon /rel, then look at the red X markers. Hardware errors show as 'Hardware error'.

options.label: It shows Hardware error or unexpected shutdown
It shows a stopped service or application failure

load_related.question: Do the restarts happen under heavy GPU or CPU load, and does the machine feel very hot first?
load_related.help: Restarts under load with high temperatures point to cooling. Restarts under load that stays cool point to power delivery.

options.label: Yes, it gets very hot first
It stays cool but still restarts
It restarts at random times too

thermal_check.question: Can you feel hot air coming out of the vents, and are the fans running loudly most of the time?
thermal_check.help: Loud constant fans and hot exhaust mean the cooling is struggling, which is common in older machines and dusty cases.

options.label: Yes, hot air and loud fans

power_or_thermal.question: Have you added any new hardware, such as a graphics card or more RAM, in the months before this started?
power_or_thermal.help: New hardware that pushes power demand beyond what the power supply can deliver causes restarts under load with no blue screen.

options.label: No upgrades, it is the same machine

result_stop_code_lookup.title: Follow the stop code guide
result_stop_code_lookup.diagnosis: A stop code names the exact driver or hardware area at fault, so you can skip straight to the likely cause.
steps: Write down the full stop code and the four parameters shown at the bottom of the blue screen
Search this site's BSOD lookup for the code or its name
Work through the ordered fix steps, which are ordered from most to least likely
Upload your minidump from C:\Windows\Minidump and we will extract the bugcheck code and parameters for you
If the code repeats after all steps, read that code's 'when to seek professional help' note for the hardware to test

result_find_minidump.title: Get the crash details from your minidumps
result_find_minidump.diagnosis: Windows saved a record of every crash. Reading it tells you the stop code even if you missed it on screen.
steps: Open File Explorer and paste C:\Windows\Minidump into the address bar
Sort by date to find the most recent .dmp files
Upload one here using the minidump analyzer, which extracts the bugcheck code and parameters safely in your browser
For more detail, install Microsoft Store WinDbg and open the dump there
Then search this site for the extracted stop code and follow its guide
Repeat for several recent files, since the same crash may record different parameters each time
warnings: Minidump files can contain fragments of your files and filenames. Treat them as private and do not upload them to public forums.
Our analyzer parses the file in memory and never stores it or runs anything from it.

result_scheduled_restart.title: Control Windows Update restarts
result_scheduled_restart.diagnosis: After installing updates, Windows schedules a restart during a maintenance window. This is expected behaviour, not a fault.
steps: Open Settings > Windows Update > Advanced options > Active hours and set your working hours
Under Advanced options > Windows Update hours, confirm the restart window
Set Restart notifications to On or Only when users are logged in, so you know before it happens

For full control, open Group Policy Editor: gpedit.msc > Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows Update > Manage settings for configuring Windows Update in Windows > No auto-restart with logon for logged-on users
Schedule active hours around your usage so the restart never interrupts you
Postpone an individual update with Pause for up to five weeks
warnings: Do not disable Windows Update permanently. Unpatched Windows is the main route for ransomware.
Restarting during a feature update rather than letting it finish can leave the system in a broken state.

result_windows_reliability.title: Read the failure in Reliability Monitor
result_windows_reliability.diagnosis: Reliability Monitor records what crashed and when, which turns guesswork into a short list.
steps: Press Win plus R, type perfmon /rel and press Enter
Look at the red X markers for the times the machine restarted
Read the 'Stop error' or 'Application name' column to identify what failed
Use our system report script to capture recent critical events into a text file you can attach to a support request
Search this site for the stop code or program name it identifies
Update the software or driver named, then check whether the restarts stop

result_overheating.title: Fix the overheating
result_overheating.diagnosis: Hardware that gets too hot throttles, then shuts down to protect itself. That shutdown looks like a random restart.
steps: Monitor temperatures while you reproduce the problem, using our hardware temperature guide
Clean dust from every fan, heatsink and radiator, since dust acts as insulation and is the most common cause
Check the CPU cooler is mounted firmly and its fan is connected and spinning freely
Confirm the case has intake and exhaust airflow and is not in a tight cupboard
Repaste the CPU cooler thermal compound after several years, using proper thermal paste
Raise the power limits slightly below thermal shutdown temperatures, or reduce them if you want it to run cooler
Replace the thermal paste on the GPU cooler if it is several years old
warnings: Do not leave thermal paste exposed to air for long periods; it can dry out. Use a proper syringe of paste.
Do not remove a heatsink while the CPU is powered. Let the machine cool fully first.
Repeated thermal shutdowns shorten CPU and GPU life. Do not ignore them.

result_psu_check.title: Check the power supply
result_psu_check.diagnosis: When new hardware pushes power demand past what the supply can deliver, machines restart or shut off under load with no error message.
steps: Check the wattage your new GPU and CPU can draw, and compare it with your power supply's rating
Remember the rating is total continuous output, and a power supply running near its limit produces unstable voltage
Test with a known-good power supply of adequate wattage, which is the only reliable test
Use a PSU load tester if you have one, or watch voltages under load with our hardware monitoring guide
Check every modular cable is fully clicked into the PSU and the same wattage's cables, since mixing cables from different supplies can destroy components
Reseat the 24-pin and CPU power connectors at both ends
warnings: Never open a power supply. The capacitors inside hold a lethal charge even when unplugged.
Only use modular cables that came with the same power supply model. Mixing cables from different units can permanently damage your hardware.
Do not buy a very cheap unbranded power supply to save money. Failing supplies destroy motherboards and GPUs.

result_ram_then_disk.title: Test memory, then the disk
result_ram_then_disk.diagnosis: On an unchanged machine, faulty RAM and a failing disk are the two hardware causes that produce restarts with no blue screen.
steps: Run MemTest86 for at least two full passes; any error at all means faulty RAM
Test one stick at a time in each slot to isolate a bad module or slot
Check the drive's SMART health using our disk health script, and back up your files
Run chkdsk C: /scan, and only then /f /r /x if the drive is healthy
Update chipset, GPU, network and storage drivers
Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth and sfc /scannow
warnings: If SMART shows failures, back up before running chkdsk with /f, since repair writes can destroy remaining recoverable data.
